In contrast, our approach involves training a single universal model to extract data from all types of documents, regardless of visual complexity, using an unconventional strategy that combines supervised learning for straightforward documents and reinforcement learning for complex ones. Through expensive manual annotation are minimized as we leverage a limited set of supervised training examples and utilize a large, publicly available set of imperfectly annotated documents as a free alternative. In tests on real-world financial documents, our system surpasses competing models with extensive annotated datasets, showcasing that significant reductions in annotation costs are possible while maintaining nearly the same level of performance.

The impending generation of powerful observatories including the LISA gravitational wave detector and third-generation ground-based detectors will yield an enormous number of signals from merging compact binaries, likely in excess of hundreds of thousands per year. These observations hold significant potential to better understand various astrophysical events, whereas a vast majority of detected signals may originate from events of small mass ratios. A key challenge will arise in distinguishing these low-mass ratio signals from background signals, likely of a different physics nature. We present a novel deep learning-based approach for automatically identifying signals from small mass ratio neutron star-black hole mergers within a wide frequency range and classifying their constituent binaries, such as neutron star-neutron star, black hole-neutron star, or black hole-black hole. Our model was trained using a wide range of signal amplitudes and was found to accurately predict binary components with a success rate of over 90% for a frequency signal-to-noise ratio of 12. When applied to simulated gravitational wave signals, our model was able to correctly identify over 93% of signals from small mass ratio neutron star-black hole mergers.

Urban residents' social interactions are crucial for maintaining mental and physical health, but the risk of COVID-19 transmission necessitated a significant reduction in these interactions. This research uses a mathematical model to evaluate the impact of reduced social connections on individuals with different incomes. It reveals that those with higher incomes, who could afford to work remotely, already had fewer social connections due to more demanding work schedules. As a result, they experienced a relatively minor decline in interactions during the pandemic. In contrast, individuals with lower incomes, who often had more social connections as part of their work, such as in public transportation or customer service, had to drastically limit these interactions. This change had a more pronounced effect on them. Furthermore, the model shows that the difference in reduced social interactions between higher and lower income individuals is significant, with low-income individuals having fewer connections available to choose from when selecting a contact network. This income-related distinction contributes to low-income individuals experiencing greater loneliness and worsening health outcomes. The model's findings are consistent with empirical research on urban residents' social interactions during the pandemic.

Three-dimensional simulations of massive young stellar objects have revealed that their surrounding disks accumulate material episodically, leading to occasional major mergers with surrounding gas. These simulations indicate that even in the presence of constant infall, there are periods where material accumulation is delayed, only to be followed by a sudden, rapid buildup of material, resulting in collisions with the surrounding environment. It is believed that such collisions could explain various phenomena associated with massive protostars, including outbursts of extreme magnitude and the formation of binary or multiple star systems. By comparing simulated spectra with actual observations, researchers have found that even in the absence of visible collisions, there may be ongoing mergers and star-stellar-merger objects that resemble binary hybrid stars, consisting of a low-mass main sequence star and a massive companion that is still in its accretion phase.

This research develops a Hamiltonian formulation of the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation, which describes how deep-water gravity waves interact with water of uniform depth and uniform vorticity, as its surface is subject to limited bandwidth and weak turbulence. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation in this context is given by $i a_t + P axx + \beta (P a_x)^2 a = 0$, where $P$ determines the wave properties, $\beta$ characterizes the vorticity, and $a$ represents the complex amplitude of the waves. This equation can be transformed into a Hamiltonian form with a modified Hamiltonian that depends on the average frequency of the waves and a new set of canonical coordinates. The Hamiltonian Dysthe equation can also be obtained from a Hamiltonian variation, which allows for an assessment of the impact of vorticity on the wave properties. The results from this approach match those from previous studies on the effects of vorticity.

For a specific class of polytopes called "locally convex terrains", we develop differential structures and compute the boundary differentials to demonstrate a generalized Stokes theorem. This involves working within the framework of differential forms that are defined on certain spaces of distributions, specifically using the Gagin's distributional approach.

Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar environments can be a complex task, depending heavily on reliable mapping and efficient path planning. While advanced path-planning algorithms can sometimes lead to performance issues, a straightforward navigation approach using a layered structure can provide a more practical solution. This structure, composed of a global map and local sonar sensors, enables rapid decision-making by prioritizing critical local information. In such a system, blending raw sonar data is a crucial pre-processing step that can significantly impact performance. By developing a new blending method that accounts for the characteristics of sonar signals and, more importantly, their impact on the navigation environment, we have enhanced our layered navigation algorithm to accurately represent the world by incorporating a precise representation of the boundaries and obstacles within the sonar's range. Experimental results from an outdoor robot navigation trial show that this approach can successfully avoid collisions and complete tasks in complex environments with limited prior mapping.

The prevalence of deceptive news poses a significant challenge to online information platforms, risking financial losses and damage to reputation. To combat this issue, techniques for detecting untrue or manipulative news are being developed. Typically, these methods leverage neural networks trained on large datasets, incorporating linguistic features and domain knowledge. However, such approaches often struggle with generalizability and tend to rely heavily on massive training data. In contrast, we propose an innovative method that leverages transfer learning from pre-trained natural language processing models to extract essential information from verified news sources, which serves as a strong basis for identifying untrustworthy news. Furthermore, we expeditiously obtain a large dataset of news articles by employing automatic text summarization, thereby expanding our existing dataset of fraudulent news articles at a rapid pace. In various experiments conducted on multiple datasets, our proposed technique consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in fraudulent news detection, demonstrating its effectiveness. In addition, we find that the generated summary of long-form text articles often yields superior performance compared to traditional techniques, which we make available for public use in our repository of code.

This research focuses on Gaussian random fields, which are used to model time series data and other geospatial systems. It identifies an inaccuracy in the existing literature concerning the behavior of these fields, specifically in regards to their local properties and variability. The problem lies in the incorrect use of second-order derivatives to measure the curvature of Gaussian random fields, as this approach leads to fields that are not mean-square continuous for natural fractal dimensions greater than 1.5. As a result, we cannot guarantee the smoothness of these fields at specific points simply because they have a high natural fractal dimension greater than 1.5. To rectify this, we propose an alternative measure of curvature using the expected value of the squared difference between a function and its linear approximation, which provides a more accurate way of assessing the behavior of these fields.

The $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis problem seeks the top-ranking orthogonal matrix $U$ that maximizes the smallest absolute directional component of the covariance matrix $\Sigma$ in an $\ell_1$-norm induced norm, making it sensitive to extreme outlier data. We have developed an iterative optimization method using projections to solve the rotationally invariant version of this problem for a given size $r$. This approach applies to data with no constraints or constraints imposed by polyhedral regions. For the unconstrained problem, we achieve a linear convergence rate, while for the constrained version, we determine that the algorithm converges. We have also numerically verified that our algorithm produces accurate results for problems with constrained data.

Traditional neural information retrieval models rely on manually curated datasets, which can be improved with the help of annotated data generated by models like BERT. We examine a unique dataset of annotated emotion-related questions, which we find to be susceptible to improvements in neural information retrieval techniques. We propose a novel approach, BERT-SAR, that leverages linguistic knowledge and reduces reliance on empirical methods. BERT-SAR comprises two primary components: a BERT-based evaluation framework and a Semantic Annotation Revision (SAR) method. The evaluation framework utilizes a BERT-based multiple classification model to categorize and prioritize queries, while the SAR method employs a knowledge-based approach to revise annotations. We further introduce two variants of BERT-SAR, guided by the degree of reliance on linguistic knowledge and neural networks. Our experiments leaseline the parameters for BERT-SAR and assess its effectiveness in revising annotations and enhancing neural information retrieval techniques. We also explore BERT-SAR's applicability to emotional language interpretation and question answering.

For robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments independently, they need to be able to construct internal maps that accurately reflect their surrounding world based on sensory data. While localisation techniques can determine the position of a pre-built map within the environment, the absence of a suitable map remains a fundamental issue. This problem is particularly pronounced in natural, dynamic, and unknown environments where it is impractical to create a comprehensive map. In response to this challenge, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, incorporating a hierarchical structure that combines local metric maps for neighbouring areas and a global topological graph for navigating the overall environment. Each map within HiTMap has a distinct purpose, ensuring consistency between the local and global maps without requiring extensive computational resources. The development of HiTMap focuses on integrating local and global map management, offering promising potential for future advancements in areas such as map synthesis, path planning, and state estimation. Experimental validation of HiTMap has been conducted using real-world navigation scenarios and simulated environments like VGLS and HiTMap is found to effectively handle dynamic alterations to unknown environments.

One of the most precise methods of measuring position variations involves atomic interferometry, capable of detecting changes as small as 1 part in 10 to the 19th factor. To further this achievement, our research proposes a novel technique where atomic beams intersect a conductive surface taking advantage of the Meissner effect, thereby enabling the measurement of strong magnetic fields in close proximity to superconducting materials. By utilizing a specific setup with atomic beam intersection near a superconducting surface, we are able to measure the change in the atomic phase due to the Meissner field, which reaches an incredible 10,000 times more than previous records, equivalent to detecting position variations of 1 part in 10 to the 13th factor. This advancement holds considerable promise for safe operation and testing of superconducting materials within quantum devices.

In this view, the underlying probabilistic geometry of finite mixture models serves as a foundation for the underlying theory. From this perspective, we can derive models and model selection methods by drawing on ideas from Choquet theory and its associated geometry. This perspective allows us to explore models and model selection through their associated probabilities, thus providing a geometric interpretation. We can further develop models and model selection via a gradient descent on the geometry of the associated probabilities. This view is demonstrated through applications to topic models and neural networks.

Developing efficient GPU code requires avoiding common GPU memory access pitfalls, such as coalescing data, minimizing bank conflicts, and aligning memory properly. To simplify this challenge, the CUDA Runtime Environment already provides a reliable memory allocator, but it cannot be used directly due to the strict requirements mentioned above. In contrast, our proposal, DynaSOAr, presents a novel, concurrent memory allocator that addresses object-oriented programming on GPUs. This allocator, which is straightforward to use, offers real-time memory allocation with automatic alignment, detects and prevents bank conflicts, and coalesces memory access within the device memory. Furthermore, DynaSOAr encompasses a stack allocator to manage small memory chunks efficiently, thus reducing memory fragmentation. This allocator is particularly useful for applications that employ dynamic memory allocation, such as simulations, games, and scientific applications. Our experiments demonstrate that DynaSOAr outperforms the standard CUDA Runtime Environment in terms of performance and surpasses a commonly used, specialized allocator in various benchmarks.

A comprehensive theoretical model has been developed to describe the spin states of magnetic adatoms or dimers on metal surfaces by employing the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) formulation within a nonequilibrium situation. This model expands on the YSR simple two-level model and incorporates spin polarization of the conduction electrons, nonequilibrium conditions, and Kondo effects. It provides the magnitude of the magnetic moment, the characteristic energy spectrum, and current-induced spin torque in a wide range of parameters. Utilizing this approach, the theoretical analysis of an individual Mn adatom and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface was performed, with comparisons to recent experiments. The proposed theory delivers accurate and detailed understanding of the YSR states and suggests that a single Mn adatom exhibits a mixed-valent behavior due to nonequilibrium conditions, whereas dimers exhibit superparamagnetic characteristics. It is also found that the YSR state in the middle band filling scenario exhibits significant stability against nonequilibrium effects, counter to earlier findings.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years based on spectral characteristics and rotational age estimates. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, we detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, the team found that the innermost planet, TOI-712.05, lies within the region that could support liquid water on its surface, making it a promising target for studying possible biosignatures.

We used hybrid DFT to investigate the magnetic and electronic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2. Notably, by analyzing the bond character of Ti and O, we found that N-tetration has a strong covalent bond, whereas C-tetration has a mixed covalent and ionic character. Additionally, N-dots exhibited a spontaneous magnetic moment of 1 $\mu_B$, whereas C-dots showed magnetic moments of both 1 $\mu_B$ and 2 $\mu_B$, depending on the calculation method. However, experimental detection of these magnetic moments may be challenging due to small magnetic moments at the surface and large diamagnetic shielding from the vast amount of O atoms.

This letter describes a novel experiment designed to detect the production of top quarks through an unseen, elastic process, which could reveal the magnitude of a particular type of particle interaction. In regular situations, when two protons collide, the resulting particles that emerge can be categorized based on various properties such as momentum velocity. However, when the time frame of these interactions is very short, multiple particles that emerge from the same interaction may not be easily identifiable as originating from a single event. By employing a specialized strategy that involves identifying a particular pattern of particle velocities, it may be possible to uncover evidence of the production of top quarks in a purely elastic process, which would allow for an accurate measurement of the strength of a fundamental particle interaction. This measurement would not only provide significant insights into the behavior of the top quark but also impact our understanding of the stability of the fundamental particle that underlies this interaction, also known as the Higgs boson. This experiment can be carried out using existing technology at the Large Hadron Collider, which operates at extremely high energies, and could yield measurable results by the end of 2026.

In the realm of Ramsey theory, an important concept is upper richness, which gauges the complexity of graphs containing specific dense substructures. This study focuses on unlimited colouring scenarios within infinite graph sequences and explores the upper richness requirements necessary to ensure a certain type of dense substructure, specifically triangles, appears in a particular coloured subgraph, regardless of how the colours are assigned. We examine how much higher than necessary complexity is needed to guarantee the occurrence of these substructures and identify specific upper bounds on this excess complexity. Additionally, we establish a key theorem regarding the upper richness required for certain odd cycle substructures to appear and offer an alternative proof for an earlier stated result.

We investigate quantum electrodynamics in (1+1)D space-time, specifically the massless scalar QED model, using qutrits in combined separate and connected architecture. When applying the combined circuit technique, we observe that certain simulations yield Qutrit-based "sound" effects, resulting from combined separate and connected circuit implementations that result in the formation of a qutrit "zero-mode" and localized photons. These calculations indicate that a critical charge exceeds the threshold required for spontaneous symmetry breaking in the connected architecture, also characterized by the presence of a zero mode. These results demonstrate that, in the combined separate and connected architecture, the development of a zero mode is indicated by the appearance of a periodic oscillation in lattice periodic boundary conditions. Furthermore, we analyze the relationship between periodization and the development of a zero mode in massless scalar QED in (1+1)D space-time.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of a partially polarized extreme ultraviolet laser on a gas-like target at room temperature. The results show that, when the laser intensity reaches 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit significant polarization, specifically up to 30 percent for a certain energy range, particularly above 2 MeV. Moreover, the simulation reveals that the degree of polarization can reach levels as high as 60 percent for positrons with energies between 2 to 10 MeV, particularly in the presence of a strong magnetic field. The production of densely packed, polarized positrons opens the door to innovative applications in physics research, such as the creation of polarized positron beams and the stabilization of particles within a storage ring.

Given a group G acting on an algebraic set defined by polynomial equations, if the diameter of G is finite, i.e., there are a number d equations with coefficients from a finite field F, defining G, then the paper shows that the group's order is contained within the dth power of the size of F. This result from [6] is improved here for finite groups without any restriction, demonstrating that the order of a finite group with diameter d can be factored into the product of d distinct prime numbers.

This research develops a compact temperature detection circuit that operates across a broad voltage range of 1.8V and provides extremely precise low-temperature detection, capable of identifying 0.24 degrees of deviation within 64SC degrees and 1.4 degrees of error in a range of 25SC degrees. The proposed design leverages both the sub-threshold voltage and threshold voltage of a MOSFET to detect small changes in temperature and includes a precise threshold voltage reference with a voltage of 0.6V, enabling efficient operation in low-power environments. The detector employs a simple, two-step conversion method for acquiring the ambient temperature, utilizing an analog-to-digital converter with a total power consumption of 5.56μW and conversion time of 63ks. The proposed design meets the requirements for low power consumption and small size in integrated systems, making it suitable for applications in the fields of healthcare, aviation, and energy management.

We introduce a new concept, geometric frameworks, which incorporates both the principles of functors and the stability properties of frameworks. This new concept is specifically tailored to operate within the context of Lie groupoids and stacks equipped with additional structure. By incorporating a notion of accuracy, geometric frameworks enable the construction of smooth groupoids and stacks through the realization of certain functors as limits of certain groupoids. This process is contingent upon specific categorical conditions being met.

A far-infrared molecular line observation made by the HIFI instrument on board the Herschel space observatory was used to analyze the core of the Dragon infrared dark nebula. This nebula, located in the constellation Monocerus, is an complex infrared dark object comprised of multiple cores. Our observation revealed a well-defined molecular ridge embracing a bright compact object within the nebula. By comparing the line intensity across the nebula, we identified a boundary indicating where the gas is transitioning from atomic to molecular phases. Two distinct cores were found: a younger core with a mass of approximately 0.5 solar masses, exhibiting rapid atomic gas fragmentation, while a more mature core of about 2.5 solar masses shows evidence of water absorption, likely due to stellar evolution heating the core. A compact object at the center of the nebula is thought to be a young open cluster containing several massive star formation candidates.

Let $\T$ be a collection of discrete random variables that are independent and identically distributed with parameters defined by a probability distribution $\pi$, and let $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k$ be discrete random variables independent of $\T$ with distribution $\pi$. We are then given the additional information that holds for the marginalized variables: the support of the marginal distribution of each $\T_i$ includes the entire support of $\pi$. Under this assumption, we may establish that the joint density function of $\T$ factorizes into the product of the densities of $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_k$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^k$, and we may identify $\lambda$ as the minimum eigenvalue of a specific matrix defined by the conditional expectations of the log-likelihood function. This discovery enables the implementation of the Metropolis-Hastings-Dial-Gelbert algorithm and the simulated annealing algorithm.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface properties, especially when they have a high interfacial tension relative to their bulk properties.  Despite the significance of this phenomenon in natural and engineering contexts, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.  This study delves into the relationship between surface tension and viscosity within foam flows, demonstrating that high viscosity leads to increased friction when the foam's texture includes irregularities.  Specifically, it was found that high viscosity leads to increased friction when the foam's texture includes irregularities, particularly in situations where the viscosity is comparable to the surface tension.  This texture-induced friction can result in unusual behaviors, such as the slowing of fluids down stairs and non-Newtonian flows within narrow channels.  This study highlights the crucial impact of surface properties on the flow of complex liquids and highlights potential applications in control systems and microfluidic devices.

This research involves developing a 2D image classification model using convolutional neural networks to diagnose skin carcinomas. A subset of the data was used to train a regularized convolutional neural network, separating it from a larger dataset that includes suspected skin carcinomas requiring further analysis. To ensure accurate representation, the trained network's output was normalized and a threshold established to categorize images as normal or abnormal. This classification model's effectiveness was assessed on a separate test dataset, demonstrating high accuracy for correctly identifying normal and abnormal images. To apply this model to the larger dataset containing outlier samples, the established threshold was used to remove obvious non-outliers, replacing the network with a decision tree to identify remaining outlier samples. This process was repeated for different dataset divisions, demonstrating consistent results. To validate the model, different dataset divisions were tested, demonstrating that the model's performance correlated with the established threshold. To further evaluate the model, independent datasets were tested, demonstrating high accuracy in comparing the established method with competing techniques.

During a fluid injection into a rotating layer of another fluid, subject to restrictions and barriers, a unique pattern of microscopic divots, called a "fish-eye" surface, can form. This phenomenon has been observed under either extremely high speed conditions or very small pressure differences, but never before has it been observed in the middle ground. In a study using clear good-quality video recordings from a Hele-Shaw cell, especially one with an adjustable curvature, "fish-eye" surface formation was found to occur in the middle ground. The condition of "fish-eye" surface formation was found to be extremely sensitive to the curvature of the cell and the rate of spinning, rather than the other factors examined, and it can be prevented from forming by introducing a perturbation, like a longitudinal barrier, that causes the interface to become curved and the pattern of divots to change from perfect symmetry.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific ethynyl cyclopentadiene variants, with a particular molecular structure, in the TMC-1 region. This finding allows for a more accurate determination of the abundances of cyano and ethynyl derivatives of cyclopentadiene and cyclopentene. Notably, the ethynyl cyclopentadiene abundance is found to be $1.2 \times 10^3$ times higher than that of ethynyl cyclopentene. This research also provides a first-time measurement of the cyclopentadiene and cyclopentene ethynyl derivatives of benzene abundances in TMC-1, with a derived ratio of $0.25$ for cyclopentadiene to cyclopentene ethynyl benzene.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that standard attention mechanisms are syntactically inflexible and cannot differentiate between pre- and post-head phrase boundaries. To address this limitation, a novel look-forward attention mechanism is proposed, targeting post-head phrase boundaries by incorporating a separate attention model for words within a dependent phrase. Furthermore, a production-based approach is explored to determine relevant words within dependent phrases by utilizing a general neural network decoder. Experimental evaluations on three language translation tasks demonstrate the look-forward attention mechanism and production-based approach consistently outperform baseline models, yielding significant improvements in translation quality.

The widespread adoption of computing grids is attributed to a primary focus on meeting societal problems head-on, ensuring seamless integration of existing technology and efficient use of existing resources. Yet, a lesser-known aspect of this success story lies in the computational economics behind it, specifically the development of grid computing as a direct application of agent-based modeling and simulation. This paper delves into the historical context of computing grids, detailing their evolution from a purely theoretical concept to a practical solution for real-world challenges. It also explores the underlying principles of economics that drove their development, presenting a comprehensive overview of the relevant technology, philosophy, and science involved.

A combined dark fluid model has been developed to explain the present day
cosmological observations. This model involves a time-dependent
cosmological constant and a fluid with a specific pressure profile that
includes a linear component, thus providing an alternative approach to
standard model predictions. The model's parameters were determined using
Hubble data and cosmic microwave background radiation, and it has been found
to align with standard model results for low redshift values. However, for
higher redshift values, the model shows distinct variations in its
cosmological analysis compared to the standard model.

Our research investigates the importance of studying J/ψ decays into a photon and nothing visible, in reference to neutrino oscillation and dark energy, which are both lacking in evidence. Although the probability of this decay happening is quite low, it could potentially provide a direct means of measuring the neutrino's type and number of types, as well as the big-bang matter density. However, we found that for at least two of the major effective dark matter models, and for all of the major photoinvisible decay modes, evidence of this process would require a J/ψ production rate that is beyond current capabilities, thereby limiting its practical use.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across distinct dimensional domains, a novel method for multivariate functional time series analysis. Based on the principles of singular spectrum analysis (SSA) and matrix approximation techniques, MFSSA can extract key information from high-dimensional time series data, even in the presence of noise. The method involves several steps, including embedding multivariate data into a high-dimensional space, applying SSA using a nearest neighbor approach, and reconstructing the original data using eigenvalues and eigenvectors from the SSA process. The effectiveness of MFSSA is demonstrated through simulations, and its application is illustrated through multivariate temperature series analysis in Australia.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of a specific stochastic process. Given a random walk with obstacles as mentioned in section 1, we examine the process's survival time, defined as the duration it takes for the walk to exit its initial domain for the second time. Our primary objectives are to study this survival time in its own right and determine its probability distribution. Furthermore, we are interested in comparing this distribution to other similar processes and determining the processes for which the walk's second exit time has an infinite expected value. Both of these analyses yield substantial results when the walk takes place within a finite domain or is bounded by specific barriers.

A detailed study of the ICRF test facility IShTAR's plasma generator has been conducted, focusing on the helicon regime. Plasma parameters were measured using a range of diagnostic tools such as Langmuir probes, camera observations, and particle flux monitors. To validate the plasma simulator, a comparison was made with established models including the helicon mode's implementation in the global ICRF simulator GIS, B3, and the plasma generator's local model PLG. This comparison showed that the parameters obtained from the experiments match those predicted by the models, with the exception of plasma sheath thickness. Additionally, an optimization of the IShTAR plasma generator's operation was suggested to maintain a stable plasma state during helicon mode.

While deep learning-based techniques have been successful in detecting cells within histopathology images, satellite structures, including cytoplasm and nuclei, have been more challenging to identify. To address this issue, a special network called W-Net has been developed, incorporating two convolutional neural networks that are designed to enhance segmentation results by fixing flaws in the input images. Experimentally, W-Net demonstrated superior performance in isolating nuclei structures within biological images, surpassing the performance of U-Net, a leading convolutional neural network. Moreover, W-Net's versatility has been showcased through its successful application in augmenting nuclei segmentation results, following inadequate segmentation output.

We prove the regional converse theorem for certain odd degree irreducible representations of $ \mathrm{SO}_ {2d+1}(q) $ and $ \mathrm{Sp}_ {2d+2}(q) $, where $q$ is a power of an odd prime number $p$, specifically those that are not realized as Galois automorphisms of the field $K$ from which the characteristic $p$ architecture is defined.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained significant traction in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align with the underlying data characteristics, thereby providing a compact and simplified representation. A detailed analysis into the relationship between GCNNs and matched filtering techniques reveals that their identical results stem from distinct, yet equivalent mathematical formulations. We validate our findings through comprehensive experimental evaluations on multiple datasets, employing GCNNs in their standard form, and an optimized matched filtering implementation tailored to their specific structure. The code for this project has been made publicly accessible via GitHub.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, a topological gravitational theory is modified to include a scalar field, resulting in the scalar field's inevitable incorporation. This modified theory, capable of accurately describing rotating black holes and solitons, is achieved through the addition of a Chern-Simons term to the action. By utilizing a conformally flat metric and assigning appropriate properties to the gauge group, this paper demonstrates how the gauge potentials can be eliminated from the field equations, which then take the form of nonlinear partial differential equations describing holonomic constraints on the gauge forces. As a result, the conservation laws for the gauge forces emerge directly from the Einstein field equations and their solutions, indicating that the Chern-Simons approach automatically enforces the conservation of the gauge forces. Moreover, this approach facilitates solutions to the field equations by eliminating the gauge forces at specific points in spacetime, thereby describing the behavior of rotating hairy black holes and solitons under conservative gauge forces.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Nonetheless, the precise measurement of liver tumors, which often present close to major blood vessels, is hindered by significant errors in ultrasound elastography, specifically in estimating the lateral displacement, where the synthetic aperture assumes a virtual origin. To address this challenge, we present a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method that reduces estimation errors near the edge of elastography images. By employing a specific synthetic aperture with a controlled curvature, the proposed VOSA technique achieves a 65% reduction in liver tumor estimation errors and outperforms the conventional method in simulated scenarios involving partial sampling. Additionally, our approach demonstrates enhanced performance in real-world data, showing a 45% improvement in tumor estimation accuracy.

Our proposed method, “Rational Pseudocode,” is a new algorithmic approach that combines human-made pseudocode with human performances on a specific task. We believe that combining these two sources of information holds significant potential for enhancing the effectiveness of algorithmic learning through observation. Human performances are linked to pseudocode through a novel connection that utilizes computational sequences and rational operations, offering a unique perspective on the problem. In our case study, we integrated pseudocode and performances to create a fully functional sorting algorithm from scratch, using just five lines of code. These results demonstrate that despite starting with minimalistic pseudocode, we can still produce scalable and efficient algorithms through a human-performance guided trial-and-error process.

In the context of high-dimensional data with a large number $n$ of points, where the dimensionality $d$ is in excess of $polylog(n)$, we develop a a a one-pass algorithm for the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem that processes an arrival stream of points within the $O(1)$-neighborhood unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$. With $k$ being the number of clusters and a specified target $\Delta$ for describing the distribution of points, the algorithm groups the points into $k$ clusters with the expected cluster description exceeding $\Omega(n \cdot \Delta^k)$, where the expected is taken over the random arrival order of points. This achievement comes as a result of combining a streaming embedding of the dynamic distribution of points in $E_d$ with a data structure called the \emph{sketch}, which enables efficient clustering without significant growth in storage usage. By utilizing the embedding and a modification of the ball tree data structure, the algorithm achieves optimal results with the option of a larger storage capacity.

Animals such as birds, insects, and reptiles engage in complex predator-prey interactions that affect their survival and evolutionary success. This RMS project leverages a simple pursuit-evasion model to explore hierarchies of strategies used by random agents in competitive games. We have already investigated a one-level framework of such games, which revealed distinct categories of winning strategies employed by the agents. In this paper, we expand upon this research by examining a multi-level pursuit-evasion game, wherein the winning strategy used by an agent varies depending on the outcome of a previous game. Our analysis uncovers a vast array of possible games, which we organize into a hierarchical structure. This hierarchical structure reveals that certain one-level winning strategies are more effective than others, a finding that can be interpreted in the context of evolutionary dynamics.

At the Heart of X-Band Collider, high-energy muon collisions will be studied in detail, resembling those found in proton collisions. In such environments, identifying vector bosons like $W$ and $Z$ is crucial for developing and refining physics research. To facilitate this, an advanced estimation method for vector boson properties has been developed, streamlining the analysis process by minimizing data processing requirements. This estimation technique, called "Semi-Sensitive Estimation," systematically tracks the distribution of vector boson properties while managing uncertainty, and has been optimized for the Heart of X-Band Collider by limiting analysis time to under 1 second per event.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using separate agents can leverage structure in task sets to improve performance, but employing a unified agent is sometimes beneficial when tasks are highly interdependent. This study investigates a similar phenomenon in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning where many tasks are interconnected and learning a single, large model is beneficial. However, there are tasks that significantly worsen the performance of others due to destructive interference, necessitating a modular system to prevent this negative effect. Our key contribution is a new algorithm that efficiently builds a modular system in a data-driven manner and prevents the detrimental impact of interfering tasks. Moreover, our analysis reveals that a unified model is suboptimal when there are tasks causing destructive interference, and we propose a lower bound on the performance gap caused by interferences. Our experimental evaluations show that our algorithm achieves superior performance compared to a unified model and often outperforms a random modular system.

We explore an interesting development where Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem leads to an unforeseen consequence - the completion of arithmetic with the standard peptide theory.  To arrive at this result, we establish a decision-making framework for peer reviewers within the standard peptide theory, which in turn requires a modified version of Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem.  This modified version is expressed in terms of the peptide theory itself, rather than its underlying arithmetic component.  One particular variant of the modified theorem is notable for its simplicity and is often referred to as the "Gathered Incompleteness Theorem".  The principles discussed here can be extended to other theories beyond arithmetic.

This paper develops a three-spheres theorem for non-homogeneous differential operators in the form of (1.1), which includes the Laplace-Beltrami operator, the Hodge operator, and the Dirac operator as special cases.

In crisis situations like natural disasters or hostilities, critical infrastructure such as communication networks, is frequently compromised, leading to a need to identify vital data within compromised networks. This task, known as posterior extraction, involves selecting the most reliable information from multiple suspect sources. I propose a novel approach to achieve this by training a specific type of generator in a way that utilizes the concept of data posterior. Specifically, I develop a customized conditional generator that utilizes two types of trainers: one that produces accurate output and another that corrects the generator's output to align with a designated criterion. I further introduce a regularization technique called the spectral scaling penalty, which enhances the generator's performance by reducing its output's scale. I demonstrate the effectiveness of my approach by applying it to real-world data, including an emergency response network and an internet network affected by an electromagnetic pulse.

This text presents an analysis of the concept of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective. We begin by introducing the basic principles and generating functions for the first-order Euler operators. We then develop a more general framework for evaluating invariant surfaces within dynamical systems of any order. This involves utilizing Euler operators and their associated characteristics. In the process, we establish specific conditions for a surface to remain invariant across a system of partial differential equations. These conditions are determined by the order of the system and are thereby bounded. Consequently, we demonstrate that in dynamical systems of order two or higher, there are no invariant surfaces except for those that are constant in nature.

The interstellar scintillation of pulsars can be an invaluable tool for studying the interstellar medium. However, this technique's effectiveness can depend heavily on observations of pulsars that exhibit both strong scintillation and accurate positions. Such a feature makes the pulsar B1133+16, located near the solar system, particularly valuable for investigating the outer reaches of the interstellar medium within 1.37 kpc of the solar system. Our investigation employed a modern approach to scintillometry, incorporating high-resolution spectroscopy and time-frequency analysis. Our main findings include the presence of scintillation patterns that indicate the Earth's velocity can cause stretching of the scintillation patterns, support previous evidence for grain-like structures within the interstellar medium, and reveal the direction of the line-of-sight component of the solar wind. Furthermore, we were able to determine the distance to the farthest scattering material along the line of sight to B1133+16 as approximately 1.25 kpc, and the angle between the normal to the interstellar electron layer and the direction to the solar system as less than 27deg.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network's conditional distribution is parameterized using an alternative method involving tanh activation functions in dilated convolution layers, enabling efficient pitch-based conditioning. Secondly, QPNet incorporates a residual channel to capture signal periodicity, further enhancing pitch sensitivity. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of QPNet in modeling periodic signal components and enabling efficient pitch control, outperforming WaveNet and its variants in various tasks, including unconditional audio generation, text-to-speech, and singing voice synthesis.

The bicategory of shadows, previously established in a 2019 paper that defined shadows as combinatorial objects, is shown to be equivalent to the bicategory of paths through a specified point in a bicategorical space. This comparison reveals that shadows possess additional structure, specifically being bicategorically bicrossed products. This extra structure is not inherent to combinatorial objects alone, suggesting that the definition of shadows should be modified to exclude this extra structure. A new definition of shadows as without this additional structure is proposed and it is demonstrated that they form a monad within the combinatorial objects. Furthermore, this extra structure is linked to the bicategory of tracks, often referred to as the classifying space of gerbes, providing a new interpretation of tracks as shadows under a specific functor.

To enhance safety and mobility for blind individuals and people in busy
environments, sound source localization beyond two dimensions is crucial.
While the human brain can achieve this task, the underlying neural mechanisms
remain unclear, particularly with respect to how it treats interfering sounds.
This study investigated EEG patterns of sound source localization in three-
dimensional space, with the focus on an important but less understood aspect
-- how the brain utilizes temporal cues. Our previous research discovered that
the hemisphere difference in sound localization plays a significant role, with
the left hemisphere dominant when there are large time differences between
sounds. In the present study, we examined EEG patterns in three-dimensional
space sound source localization with varying time differences between sounds
and found that the right hemisphere exhibited less dominant activity compared
to the left hemisphere, except in the analysis of three-dimensional sound
source localization with a small time difference between sounds. Furthermore,
our findings were consistent across both monaural and binaural hearing tests.
Our findings are expected to contribute to the development of effective sound
source localization algorithms in noisy environments.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks (GNNs) have been propelled by the massive amount of data being generated and the importance of scaling to large graphs. Despite these achievements, several key challenges remain, including the substantial computational cost, memory requirements, and GNN model training difficulties, particularly in models using deformation capabilities. These issues stem from the complex and inefficient nature of traditional graph convolution operations. Building upon the fundamental concept of graph convolution, we present a novel type of graph convolution called the Lorentzian graph convolution, characterized by a precise analysis of its frequency response. This analysis reveals that Lorentzian graph convolutions operate under specific frequency rejection characteristics, allowing them to efficiently process small-scale local networks efficiently. We also introduce a simple yet effective GNN model called Lorentzian GNN (LGNN), incorporating Lorentzian graph convolutions, designed to tackle small-sized intrinsic networks. Our experiments show that LGNN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmark datasets, consistently delivering superior performance while significantly reducing training costs and memory consumption.

This research undertakes a numerical investigation of a hole in a canvas holding air, using mathematical models that combine fluid dynamics and elasticity. The study examines how a moving object outside the canvas affects the air within it. Unlike similar studies, the object's movement is unknown and must be deduced from measurements of the air's movement. A numerical method is developed to estimate the object's movement based on the mathematical equations and measurements, by comparing the computer-simulated air movements with the real ones. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated by applying it to the numerical model of the computer simulations.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model based on the Tsallis entropy concept, and explore the framework's implications. This entropy framework, which can be adjusted to accommodate different reference states, serves as a foundation for our model. As a result, our model encompasses both the exponential and the hyperbolic delay discounting models when specific reference states are employed. Consequently, our model's parameters have a clear, intuitive interpretation. Furthermore, we derive the opportunity cost function for our model and demonstrate that its inflection point coincides with the threshold for impulsivity versus impulsventness. Implications for future research are also discussed.

We are presenting a summary of harmonic gauge theories within the framework of massive gravity, which encompasses linearized gravity and its extended versions. This summary focuses on the fundamental principles and mechanisms underlying these theories, and it highlights the key roles that harmonic gauge symmetries and massive scalar fields play in them. A comprehensive review of the existing literature on these theories is also presented in this summary.

A modified version of the Weyl-Wigner representation of the canonical equations of thermodynamic equilibrium in a quantum system is introduced. This version uses Weyl-Wigner representations of both the canonical equations and the H-theorem. The standard Weyl-Wigner representation of the canonical equations includes an additional symmetry under a global gauge transformation. The classical limit of the modified version reduces to the standard Liouville condition and the Euler equation, respectively. The modified version is related to a complex Lagrange multiplier and involves a precise characterization of the phase space operator algebra. The Weyl-Wigner representation of the H-theorem involves a Poisson bracket with a Hamiltonian operator, which is used to derive the classical limit of the H-theorem. The modified version is also associated with the irreversibility of a quantum system through the Wigner function's monotonic behavior with respect to a quantum version of the Boltzmann distance.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been understood for nearly a century, since the work of Boltzmann, Einstein, and Lindberg. Since its inception, this concept has undergone significant development, inspired by the famous 1999 experiment by which a high-velocity ionized hydrogen gas was produced at a "negative" absolute temperature of approximately 1088K. This robust construct has found applications in both the solid state and the realm of relativistic particle physics. Notably, it has been incorporated into the fundamental theories of quantum field on curved spaces and of many-body interplay, where it has facilitated a deeper understanding of certain phenomena, such as the formation of quark gluon plasma and the behavior of fermions within solid matter, including semiconductor systems and heavy metal alloys.

Within the most fundamental scoto-seesaw framework, we examine the underlying dynamics of fermion mass generation and dark matter phenomena. In this context, we establish a basic set of assumptions that enable the development of dark sector Lagrangians, separating the fundamental scalar and fermion sectors by a TeV-scale mediator. By integrating these sectors through a TeV-scale operator, we obtain the effective dark matter Lagrangian and verify that it conforms to the operator hierarchy originally defined. Consequently, we can determine the effective dark matter mass term and identify a minimal set of relevant operators that dictate dark matter phenomena. Here, we specifically investigate the case of minimal dark left-handed charged scalar doublet. Under this scenario, we determine the relevant operator hierarchy, determine the dark matter mass matrix, and examine the operator hierarchy to ensure consistency with experimental data. Furthermore, we explore the parameters that influence the anomalous magnetic moment of dark matter particles and determine the conditions for vacuum stability in the dark sector. Additionally, we examine the conditions for WIMP dark matter density and modify the operator hierarchy to accommodate these requirements. Finally, we outline the parameters that dictate vacuum stability and provide a suitable parameter hierarchy to ensure data consistency.

We use a one-band Hubbard model to investigate the orbitally degenerate $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ $d$-electron case, varying the ratio of on-site Hubbard interaction to bandwidth and spin-orbit coupling. Calculations are performed numerically using a exact diagonalization method for a honeycomb lattice with nearest and next-nearest neighbor interactions. Our results show that the one-band and multi-band descriptions converge in favor of a one-band model in calculations of magnetic properties for 3d, 4d, and 5d materials, including transition temperatures, magnetic moments, and band widths. The one-band model accurately replicates the spatial polarization of the $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ bands, which differs due to the relative strengths of on-site interaction and spin-orbit coupling. The one-band approach also captures the interband and intraband interactions that give rise to the spreading of the magnetic moment with temperature or on-site interaction. Furthermore, we determine the one-band bandwidths for various materials, incorporating effects of lattice dimensions, on-site interaction, spin-orbit coupling, and d-electron occupation. A simple effective one-band model is proposed to analyze these results.

We establish a foundation for the relative quantum topological invariant in a specific context, building on Khovanov's homology and Kapustin's formulation of TQFT. This inductive framework applies to a class of closed, oriented surfaces that arise from linked collections of hinges and whose ambient space varies. These surfaces fit into a specific type of singular surface described by equations, which enables the creation of a graph representing its topological characteristics. This graph can be obtained through modifications to a base graph composed of planar regions, each corresponding to a specific surface element. We develop a method for developing relative Khovanov-Rozansky invariants under alterations to the surface's ambient space, which includes adding or removing holes and changing surface singularities. Specifically, we can add a single surface singularity with an arbitrary Euler characteristic or remove a single singular point, among other modifications. These changes can be achieved through a sequence of such alterations to the initial base graph.

Chest X-rays are a widely used diagnostic tool for detecting diseases like pneumonia, but their subjectivity makes them difficult to interpret, especially for conditions like ALI (Acute Lung Injury) and ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome). To enhance the accuracy of these interpretations, an innovative approach is proposed to enhance specific features of X-rays based on their corresponding medical reports. This method identifies regions of interest on the X-rays and evaluates their relationship to medical report data, prior to applying transformation techniques to optimize the images for better model performance. In particular, a novel approach is proposed to extend the ChestX-ray Disease Classification Challenge dataset to include image modification guided by clinical severity, resulting in a new standard for evaluating and training machine learning models for diagnosing lung diseases from X-rays. Experimental evaluations using both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and provide valuable insights into hyperparameter configuration and model performance.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data analysis, specifically designed for the visual examination of high-dimensional vectors. It allows users to project data across various low-dimensional spaces via different manifold learning techniques and provides interactive features to further analyze the data. With customizable 2D visualizations and advanced tools for clustering and sorting data, ViDaExpert facilitates the evaluation of both supervised and unsupervised learning models. The application supports multiple input data formats and offers a simple, user-friendly interface for easy navigation. ViDaExpert is useful for a range of applications including the assessment of machine learning models, as well as nonlinear dimension reduction techniques, and can be run on multiple operating systems.
